title: How to Stop Revenge Bedtime Procrastination and Keep Your Evening

copy.cover_headline: Keep your evening. Change how it ends.

points.headline: The evening isn't the problem
points.body: Wanting time to yourself at night is reasonable. The feed is the problem: it has no natural end and keeps your body on alert long after you've stopped enjoying it.

points.headline: Notice: still scrolling, not enjoying it
points.body: Your cue is a feeling, not the clock. Jaw tight, shoulders creeping up, thumb moving but you couldn't name the last three things you saw.

points.headline: Reset: three 4-6 breaths
points.body: In gently through your nose for 4, out slowly for 6. Three times, about 30 seconds. No holds, no gulping. It should feel like a long, unhurried sigh.

points.headline: Switch to a last thing you chose earlier
points.body: Pick it while you still have self-control: a few pages of a book, five minutes of floor stretches, or a podcast on a sleep timer. Then put the phone across the room.

points.headline: Drifted back? Do one more reset
points.body: That's not a failure. Guilt winds you up too. One more round of breaths, then go to your last thing. One downshift that works beats a strict plan dropped by Wednesday.

reel_lines: Your thumb keeps moving. The fun stopped a while ago.
Your jaw is tight and bedtime keeps slipping.
A few slow exhales bring you back down.
copy.instagram_caption:
Still scrolling at 11:40 but no longer enjoying it? That's your off-ramp.

Breathe in gently through your nose for 4, out slowly for 6. Do it three times, about 30 seconds, no holds. Then switch to a calm last thing you picked earlier: a book, some stretches, a podcast on a sleep timer. Phone across the room.

You keep the me time. You just change how it ends.

copy.facebook_message:
Revenge bedtime procrastination is staying up later than you planned because late night feels like the only time that's yours. Wanting that time is reasonable. The feed is what stretches one hour into three.

Instead of a strict bedtime, try a check-in. Set an alarm 30 to 45 minutes before you want to be asleep. When it goes off, ask whether you're enjoying the scroll or just still there. Then breathe in for 4 and out for 6, three times, and switch to a calm last thing you chose earlier, like a book or a few stretches.

The full guide covers what the research says and a 60-second evening script you can use tonight.
